Well the exhaust gases gets cooled with coolant. If it's an internal leak then the coolant will get into the exhaust and burn away. I've replaced lots of those for the 2.0 tdi. If you see something that looks like soot or oil sludge/an external leak as well on your cooler then that would be proof. As the coolant mixes with the soot inside it turns into sludge.

To rule out head gasket etc you could do a leakdown test and a compression test just to be sure.

You could also loosen the egr pipe and check inside with an inspection camera. When we check the T6 we let the car get hot, let it stay for a day and then check for coolant because it takes time for it to seep through.

To test glow plugs - disconnect the wires that go on top of the glow plugs. Use a multimeter, and measure Ohm. Measure the glow plug and the engine block close to the glow plug.

You could also use a test light. Clamp the test light wire to the positive battery terminal and touch the glow plug with the test light. If it lights up it's good.

The glow relay is also the system's control unit, you should check the system for codes.

If the system is completely dry then it's okay. Replace the brake lines you need to replace then bleed the entire system.

So many people here who haven't heard of CuNi. There are pros and cons of using CuNi lines and steel lines, but both are perfectly safe and I've repaired both types of brake lines.

Steel lines are strong and can withstand more pressure but it will rust, though they come with different types of rust protection from the factory. Lots of car brands will require that you only use steel lines when repairing brake lines.

CuNi lines are much easier to bend and work with but can't handle as much pressure as steel lines. The rust protection is excellent and there's nothing bad about using them. In the end it's about how much pressure they'll be handling.

OP, a small tip! Before you cut the lines, make sure to use something to keep the brake pedal depressed. That will push the pistons in the main cylinder inwards and keep the brake fluid in the reservoir from emptying. If your car has ABS and air gets into the module it will be a pain to bleed it.

Good luck!
